description: Replay scenarios. Each runs its `steps` in order against a fresh state and then checks `expect`. A step is either a transaction (`tx`), a bare height advance (`advanceTo`), or a `check` against the state at that point. A `check` may also carry `label`, which snapshots the four §8.1 component digests (`nameRoot`, `pricesRoot`, `pendingRoot`, `unreservedRoot` — the commitment minus the height and the log hash), and `since` + `changed`, which compares them against an earlier label: every component **not** listed in `changed` MUST be byte-identical. `logLines` is the number of §8.2 lines emitted so far, and a height advance MUST never add one.

scenarios.note: The named conformance case from §14. Albatross includes failed transactions in blocks; without §7.5's first rule a failed G takes a name, and two implementations disagreeing produce different roots.
The ordinary case: most chain traffic is not NNS. It earns no log line at all (§7.6).
The long band is cheaper, but a standard-band name priced at the long-band fee is still underpaid.
§7.4: the status and its end height are provable from the checkpoint tree, so a correct client prevents this.
§5.3: the owner cannot name themselves as recipient, so PROTOCOL_ADDRESS carries the operation.
§7.3: owner and target both become the new owner, host cleared, offers cancelled, pending X void.
§7.4 lists no such reason. The value at stake is DUST_VALUE; the code records why the message had no effect. See docs/decisions.md.

r20 removed `R` and the recovery address. There is no second, slower transfer path: an `X` from anyone but the current owner forfeits NOT_OWNER, and the owner's own `X` matures on XFER_TIMELOCK. Replaces r19's recovery_transfer_uses_the_longer_timelock.

steps.note: one block short of XFER_TIMELOCK from 58842722

scenarios.note: §6 N: not from the renewal height, so early renewal is never penalised. Sender: anyone.

expect.note: The buyer inherits the name's current expiry, and the two legs sum to the price exactly.

scenarios.note: §6 O: the price MUST be ≥ MIN_PRICE, which is FEE_LONG at the message's height — 40000000 luna here. The four rejected prices are the ones a token floor would have admitted: 0 (no B can satisfy it, §5.4 rejects value: 0), 1 (the token floor considered and rejected), REFUND_FLOOR - 1 (a losing bidder would be forfeited, not refunded, contradicting §7.4), and 19 (floor(19 × 5%) = 0, erasing the AUCTION_MIN_INCREMENT rule). The floor itself is accepted: the boundary is inclusive.

MIN_PRICE is defined as FEE_LONG, not as a luna amount, so a P that moves FEE_LONG moves the floor with it at its effective height. An implementation reading the launch constant instead of the active params passes every other vector here and diverges from this one.

§7.3: effects due at height H fire before block H's transactions. Both G messages sit in block 58885920, the P's own effective height — so both are priced at the new FEE_STANDARD, and the one paying the old fee forfeits. An implementation that applied the activation after the block would accept the first and reject the second.

PRICE_MAX_FACTOR and PRICE_MIN_INTERVAL were removed (§10.6), so a P may move a band as far as it likes and land in the very next block. What is left is the range check: one luna above PRICE_CEILING forfeits, and the active prices are unchanged.

§6 `P`: a P accepted while another is pending replaces it — §8.1 commits at most one pending P, and it is the most recently accepted. Reachable a block apart since r20 removed PRICE_MIN_INTERVAL, so the two readings (queue or replace) would otherwise diverge in pendingRoot immediately and in pricesRoot at the first effective height. An implementation that queues applies 400000000 at 58929120.

By protocol version, not by omission: an implementation that honoured A would derive a different root, so v1 conformance requires this same forfeit. §6 A gives the reserve the same MIN_PRICE floor as an O price, but no A reaches that check in v1 — a below-floor reserve still answers AUCTION_NOT_IN_V1, because a different reason code here would change the log and therefore the checkpoint (§8.2).
binance is on the published half of RESERVED_NAMES, a §3 constant since the launch freeze — the scenario overrides no config.
web3 is on no published list — 1-4 character names satisfying rules 2-5 are RESERVED_NAMES members by rule (§4.1, r18). Released, the floor no longer binds and a G registers it at the normal fee.

An awarded short name is REGISTERED at effective_height without passing through AVAILABLE (§6 U, §7.3); the activation runs before the block's transactions, so a prepared G loses the race and is refunded.
ab- fails rule 4, so it is on neither §4.1 membership route: never reserved, never releasable. The r18 revert widened U to well-formed short names only.
§7.3 fixes no order for effects due at the same height, and the two readings disagree: expire-first would cancel the pending X as part of the grace reset. See docs/decisions.md.

§6 `O`: an offer auto-expires *at* `opened_height + OFFER_MAX_LIFETIME`. The crossing moves the pending root and nothing else — the name tree is identical on both sides — so an indexer that published only a name root could not see it at all, and one that fired a block early would agree with everyone on all 27 §7.4 tokens while committing a different pending root for 1,296,000 blocks.

scenarios.note: §6 `X`: "Takes effect at `height + XFER_TIMELOCK`" — measured from the block the `X` landed in, not from the registration. The timelock is the window in which the owner may still cancel with a `K`, so firing a block early shortens the only protection `X` offers.

scenarios.note: §6 `P`: the change binds *at* `effective_height`, which MUST be at least the landing block + `GOVERNANCE_DELAY` — 86,400 since r20 doubled it. Pinned here with a bare advance rather than by pricing a `G`, so it holds for a quiet stretch with no traffic at all: the prices root and the pending root move together, one dropping the pending `P` as the other adopts it.

steps.note: one block short: the old prices still bind
exactly GOVERNANCE_DELAY after the P landed

scenarios.note: §6 `U`, release row: at `effective_height` the name leaves RESERVED_NAMES and is AVAILABLE. This is the r16 hole at its exact height — a released name has no leaf and no pending entry, so the name root is byte-identical across the crossing and only tag 0x0A's unreserved root records that anything happened.

steps.note: one block short: binance is still reserved

scenarios.note: §6 `U`, award row: at `effective_height` the name becomes REGISTERED with `expiry = effective_height + TERM_LENGTH` — the awardee's term runs from the moment the award binds, not from the block the `U` landed in. Both numbers moved in r20 (GOVERNANCE_DELAY doubled, TERM_LENGTH fell to 31,536,000), so this pins the arithmetic on either side of the effect.

steps.note: one block short: no leaf yet, and BOB owns nothing

scenarios.note: Both ends of §7.3's REGISTERED → GRACE → AVAILABLE chain, each pinned at its own height. §6 `G` fixes `expiry = block_height + TERM_LENGTH` and §7.3 draws the arrows, but neither says in words whether the arrow fires *at* `expiry` or after it — the reading here is the one that makes TERM_LENGTH a length: the term is [registration, expiry-1], exactly 31,536,000 blocks, and GRACE is [expiry, expiry+GRACE_PERIOD-1], exactly 2,592,000. Same half-open form §6 `X` and §6 `U` state outright with "at". Both constants moved in r20, and the delegate host clearing (§7.3) is pinned to the same block as the status change.

scenarios.note: The user-visible consequence of the boundary above, and the one place a single block decides whether a name is recoverable. `kikename` is renewed on the last block of grace and survives; `othername`, identical in every way, is renewed one block later and takes NAME_NOT_FOUND — the release fired before that block's transactions (§7.3), so by the time the `N` is read there is no record to extend. §6 `N` extends from the current expiry, not from the renewal height, which is why the survivor's new expiry is expiry + TERM_LENGTH and not renewal + TERM_LENGTH.

checkOrder.description: Check precedence. Each case is a message that satisfies **two** rejection conditions at once; `verdict` is the token the earlier check produces and `insteadOf` is the same probe rebuilt to trip only the later one, which MUST earn the other token. Both run against the state left by `setup`, named from `setups`. The pair is the assertion: swap the two checks in a reducer and the first expectation fails, delete the later check and the second does. `pinnedBy` names the clause that fixes the order, or is `null` where the order is an implementation choice with nothing behind it — read those before reordering anything. `insteadOfUnreachable` replaces `insteadOf` where the later token cannot be produced at all.

cases.note: Albatross puts failed transactions in blocks. §7.5 discards one before the message is parsed, so it earns no log line at all — a reducer that routed first would write a WRONG_RECIPIENT line no other implementation has.
The network check is first of all, and is the one §7.5 rule that does not even advance the state's height. This payload would forfeit three different ways on mainnet.

The same rule against the *parse*, which is the half the routing pair cannot see: a failed transaction carrying a payload that does not parse must still be discarded silently, not logged as MALFORMED_PAYLOAD. §7.5 runs "before a message is even parsed".

§7.4 puts an unknown type, an unparseable payload and a 64-byte overrun in one bullet without ordering them, but they are three different tokens. `parse` measures the length before it reads the type letter. Unreachable on mainnet — 65 bytes never lands in a block — so this pair exists only here.
Both payloads are empty after the type letter. The type is read first, so an unknown letter is reported as such rather than as a payload that failed to parse.

A `D` with no pipe does not parse, and it is also at the wrong address. Routing is a §5.3 property of a parsed message, so it cannot precede the parse — but nothing states that, and the two tokens differ.

cases.note: Fourth and fifth — the case §7.4 spells out in words: "An underfunded `G` for an already-taken name therefore forfeits". This is the only place the spec puts a forfeit ahead of a refund, and the money goes to different places under the two readings.

cases.pinnedBy: §7.4 — "recipient, name syntax, reservation, value, then availability"
cases.note: Fourth and fifth again, on the other branch of availability: a name in GRACE rather than one held by somebody else.

§7.4 lists "`X`, `S`, `D` on an expired or grace-period name" and "`S`, `O`, `D`, `X`, `K` from anyone other than the current owner" as two bullets, in that order, but a bullet list is not a check order. A stranger's `S` on a grace name trips both.

§7.4 lists "`X`, `S`, `D` on an expired or grace-period name" and "`S`, `O`, `D`, `X`, `K` from anyone other than the current owner" as two bullets, in that order, but a bullet list is not a check order. A stranger's `X` on a grace name trips both.
`D` is the only message with both a routing check and a tighter payload limit; routing runs first.
Same unordered pair of §7.4 bullets as `S` and `X`.

This is the whole of what carries `INVALID_HOST`: the host is validated **last**, after ownership. A reducer that checked the host first would give a stranger's malformed `D` the host token instead, and §7.4 says nothing either way — the two are separate bullets.
Routing before existence: §5.3 sends every `K` to `PROTOCOL_ADDRESS`, and that is read before the registry is consulted at all.
Existence before ownership: a stranger's `K` for a name nobody holds reports the name, not the sender.
Ownership before the thing being cancelled. Nothing is pending on `kikename` in either message; only the sender differs.
Routing before existence, as for `K` — but an `N` is fee-bearing, so it goes to the treasury rather than to `PROTOCOL_ADDRESS`.

`N` puts existence ahead of value. §7.4 fixes that order for `G` and says nothing about `N`, so the consistency is a choice — but a reducer that reversed it would answer an underfunded renewal of a nonexistent name with the value token.
Routing before ownership. §5.3 sends an `O` to the treasury, since it is a fee-bearing message even at a `LISTING_FEE` of zero.

This is what carries `BELOW_MIN_PRICE`: the floor is checked after ownership. §7.4 pins the floor against the *value carried* — "The payload is checked before the value carried" — and says nothing about the sender. That value ordering is unobservable today, since `LISTING_FEE` is 0 and no `O` can underpay, so this pair is the only live precedence the token has.
Routing before the offer lookup. A `B` at the treasury never reaches the marketplace's books, so it forfeits rather than earning a refund.

cases.pinnedBy: §7.4 — "An amount below `REFUND_FLOOR` is forfeited rather than refunded"
cases.note: The floor converts a refund into a forfeit, so it is read after the refund reason is settled and overrides its token. Both sides of the pair are the same message at two values.
The other refund arm, against a genuinely open offer.

§6 `A` says every `A` takes `AUCTION_NOT_IN_V1`, and routing nonetheless runs first — an `A` at the treasury earns `WRONG_RECIPIENT`. Defensible (§5.3 routing precedes every type's own rules) but genuinely unstated, and the clause reads as though it admits no exception.

A reserve of one luna is far below `MIN_PRICE`, and the message still takes the version forfeit: §6 requires *every* `A` to earn this token, so a below-floor one earning `BELOW_MIN_PRICE` would put a different reason in the log than a conforming implementation.
cases.insteadOfUnreachable: No `A` reaches the floor check in v1, by §6's own requirement, so `BELOW_MIN_PRICE` is unreachable for `A` rather than merely later.

cases.note: Routing before authority. §5.3 puts a `P` at `PROTOCOL_ADDRESS`; the sender is only consulted once the message is at the right address.
Authority before notice. §7.4's `P` bullet names the sender and the §10.6 bounds, and puts notice in a trailing sentence covering `P` and `U` together — no order anywhere.

Notice before the §10.6 rails. The `fee_standard` here is 200,000 NIM, twice `PRICE_CEILING`, and the notice is one block — a fat-fingered governance message that is also badly timed reports the timing.
Authority first, even for the one recipient `U` forbids.

**This one contradicts §7.4's prose.** The clause lists a `U`'s forfeits as "from any sender other than `ADMIN_ADDRESS`, with less than `GOVERNANCE_DELAY` notice, awarding to `BURN_ADDRESS`, …" — notice ahead of the recipient. The reducer checks the recipient first, on the argument that the recipient decides which of two operations the message even is (§6 `U`: `PROTOCOL_ADDRESS` releases, anything else awards). Both are defensible; the list is prose rather than a stated order, and this vector is the only thing standing behind the choice.
Notice before the name. `ab-` is three characters with a trailing hyphen, so it fails §4.1 rules 2–5 and is on neither membership route.
Name syntax before reservation, matching the order §7.4 fixes for `G`. Neither `ab-` nor `kikename` is reserved, so the first would earn `NAME_NOT_RESERVED` too under the other reading.
Routing before authority, the same way `P` does it.
